title: God Is Our Refuge and Strength
superscription: For the choirmaster. Of the sons of Korah. According to Alamoth. A song.

verses.text: God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in times of trouble.
Therefore we will not fear, though the earth is transformed and the mountains are toppled into the depths of the seas,
though their waters roar and foam and the mountains quake in the surge. Selah
There is a river whose streams delight the city of God, the holy place where the Most High dwells.
God is within her; she will not be moved. God will help her when morning dawns.
Nations rage, kingdoms crumble; the earth melts when He lifts His voice.
The LORD of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress. Selah
Come, see the works of the LORD, who brings devastation upon the earth.
He makes wars to cease throughout the earth; He breaks the bow and shatters the spear; He burns the shields in the fire.
"Be still and know that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted over the earth."
The LORD of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress. Selah

context.author: The title names the sons of Korah, a family of Levites descended from the Korah who rebelled against Moses (Numbers 16). His sons did not die with him (Numbers 26:11), and their descendants became gatekeepers and singers at the Temple (1 Chronicles 9:19; 2 Chronicles 20:19).
context.genre: Psalm: a song or prayer in Hebrew poetry
context.audience: Israel at worship in Jerusalem, and every reader who prays
context.setting: “God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in times of trouble. Therefore we will not fear, though the earth is transformed and the mountains are toppled into the depths of the seas” (vv.1-2). Against the roaring waters stands a quiet river: “There is a river whose streams delight the city of God, the holy place where the Most High dwells. God is within her; she will not be moved” (vv.4-5). Nations rage, but He speaks and the earth melts (v.6). The refrain: “The LORD of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress” (vv.7, 11). “Come, see the works of the LORD” (v.8): He ends wars and burns the weapons (v.9). God Himself speaks: “Be still and know that I am God” (v.10).
context.custom: Jerusalem had no great river, only the Gihon spring, whose water Hezekiah brought into the city by tunnel before the Assyrian siege (2 Kings 20:20). “When morning dawns” (v.5) may recall the morning when the Assyrian army was found dead outside Jerusalem (2 Kings 19:35). Alamoth (title) may mean ‘young women,’ perhaps a high voice range.
context.timelineImmediate: Psalm 47 calls all peoples to clap their hands for God the King.
context.timelineBible: Martin Luther based the hymn ‘A Mighty Fortress Is Our God’ (1529) on this psalm. The refrain “The LORD of Hosts is with us” recalls the name Immanuel, which means “God with us” (Matthew 1:23; Isaiah 7:14). Revelation pictures the river of life flowing through the city of God (Revelation 22:1-2).

translation.meaning: Help, assistance; God is “an ever-present help.”
To let go, relax, stop; “cease striving.”

gospelParallels.note: Immanuel, which means God with us.
The river of the water of life.
A kingdom that cannot be shaken.

otBackground.note: The Assyrian army struck down outside Jerusalem.
A river flows from the Temple.

overview.summary: Though the earth shakes and nations rage, God is His people’s refuge and the river that gladdens His city; He ends wars and says, “Be still and know that I am God.”
overview.settingLine: A city with a quiet river amid raging waters.

archaeology.t: Carved to bring the Gihon spring into the city.
Tells how the tunnelers met in the middle.

overview.discussion: “Be still and know that I am God” (v.10). What would it mean for me to stop striving and let God be God?
overview.book: The book of Psalms · 150 psalms (1-100 in the app so far). Israel’s songs and prayers: praise, lament, thanks, trust and wisdom, many of them by David.
overview.author: The sons of Korah
overview.audience: God’s people in a shaking world
